newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain spy goes on trial for leaking secret files.
newsitem.headline: Spain spy goes on trial for leaking secret files.

text.p: Spain's former head of covert operations went on trial on Monday accused of stealing and leaking classified documents in a case that rocked the secret service and helped lead to the downfall of the former Socialist government.

Colonel Juan Alberto Perote faces charges of stealing hundreds of top-secret files, including some vital to state security and others that implicate the former Socialist government in a "dirty war" against Basque separatists in the 1980s.

Dressed in army attire and appearing weary after two years in and out of jail and under the spotlight, Perote arrived at a military court in the capital to testify on the first day of the closed-door trial.
The former secret service number two, who is accused of peddling the documents to newspapers, businessmen and parties interested in undermining the Socialists, faces a total of 10 years in prison.
He denies the charges and claims the documents were inadvertently put into his briefcase when he was fired in 1991.
Perote headed the Operative Group of the CESID military intelligence unit, which handled the Defence Ministry's most sensitive security cases, for nine years.
The compromising files record briefings Perote held with his boss, CESID head Lt-General Emilio Alonso Manglano, on clandestine operations.

The documents purportedly show that former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez and his associates were reponsible for setting up undercover squads to combat the separatist violence of Basque guerrilla group ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom).
The so called Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL) killed 28 people in Basque areas of southwest France between 1983 and 1987.
The papers also provide details of a bugging scandal in which the secret service tapped the telephones of a number of prominent politicians, businessmen, judges and even King Juan Carlos.

The scandals led to a raft of resignations including a deputy prime minister, defence minister and Manglano. They tainted the Socialists in the eyes of the Spanish public and contributed to their election defeat in March 1996 after more than 13 years in power.
Perote is believed to have microfilmed the documents and destroyed a large part of the originals six months before he was fired. But he denies he deliberately stole the files.
Officials say Perote eventually returned the files, although it is not clear whether what he handed back were originals or legally worthless copies.
He was arrested in June 1995 after the anti-Socialist newspaper El Mundo published excerpts from the documents.

Copies of the documents were later found during a court search of Perotes's prison cell. In a desperate attempt to destroy the evidence he crammed some of the papers in his mouth and tried to swallow them, judges said.
The papers have remained classified by request of the previous Socialist government and the current conservative administration, who argue that they contain state secrets.

But judges investigating the "dirty war" say the documents contain vital evidence against senior Socialists, including Gonzalez, and in April the Supreme Court overturned a previous decision and ordered the government to declassify 13 files.
In a recent interview with El Mundo, Perote said Gonzalez was aware of and responsible for the death squads.
The former prime minister has consistently denied any knowledge of or involvement in the GAL and the Supreme Court has ruled that evidence so far does not justify questioning the Socialist leader.
